QUESTION: Which of the three tariffs (Fixed, Variable or Time-of-use) will give the household the lowest total energy bill over the next 12 months, and by how much? DATA: A household is choosing an energy tariff for the next 12 months (365 days). It is currently on the Variable tariff and can switch freely: none of the tariffs below has an exit fee. Last 12 months' usage: electricity 3,100 kWh, gas 12,000 kWh. About 15% of the household's current electricity use falls in the off-peak window (dishwasher and washing machine on timers). The household takes delivery of an electric car next week. It expects to need about 2,400 kWh a year of home charging, all of which it will schedule in the off-peak window. Gas use is not expected to change. | Tariff | Electricity unit rate | Electricity standing charge | Gas unit rate | Gas standing charge | | Fixed (F) | 24.5p/kWh | 55p/day | 6.2p/kWh | 30p/day | | Variable (V) | 22.0p/kWh | 60p/day | 6.0p/kWh | 31p/day | | Time-of-use (E) | 30.0p/kWh peak; 8.0p/kWh off-peak (00:30-05:30) | 50p/day | 6.0p/kWh | 31p/day | Rates on V can change at the supplier's discretion with 30 days' notice; the supplier has announced no change. F and E are fixed for 12 months. Ignore VAT (rates already include it). Here is your current analysis: # Energy Tariff Comparison for the Next 12 Months ## Answer **The Time-of-use tariff (E) gives the lowest bill: £2,035.35 for the year.** That is **£226.80 less than staying on Variable (V)**, which costs £2,262.15, and £366.40 less than Fixed (F), which costs £2,401.75. I rechecked every figure in the previous version and they are correct. The changes below fix one overstated claim and tighten the robustness section. ## What changed from the previous version 1. **The claim "F is never the best choice" was too strong.** F beats E if more than about 1,665 kWh of the car's charging happens at peak times. In that case V beats both of them, unless V's rates rise. The accurate statement is that F only wins if two things go wrong at once: V's rates rise and the charging plan fails. 2. **The V rate-cut threshold now gives an exact figure.** The unit rate would need to fall to about 17.9p, not just "under 18p". It would also need to fall further if the cut came part-way through the year. 3. **I added a check that the 5-hour off-peak window is long enough for the charging.** It is. 4. **I noted that the car arrives next week,** so charging over the 12 months may be about 2% below the 2,400 kWh annual estimate. This changes nothing material. ## Usage for the next 12 months | | Peak | Off-peak | Total | |---|---|---|---| | Existing use (3,100 kWh, 15% off-peak) | 2,635 | 465 | 3,100 | | Car charging (all off-peak) | 0 | 2,400 | 2,400 | | **Total electricity** | **2,635** | **2,865** | **5,500** | | Gas | | | 12,000 | ## Costs (365 days) | | Fixed (F) | Variable (V) | Time-of-use (E) | |---|---|---|---| | Electricity units | 5,500 × 24.5p = £1,347.50 | 5,500 × 22.0p = £1,210.00 | 2,635 × 30p = £790.50
2,865 × 8p = £229.20 | | Electricity standing charge | 55p × 365 = £200.75 | 60p × 365 = £219.00 | 50p × 365 = £182.50 | | **Electricity total** | **£1,548.25** | **£1,429.00** | **£1,202.20** | | Gas units | 12,000 × 6.2p = £744.00 | 12,000 × 6.0p = £720.00 | £720.00 | | Gas standing charge | 30p × 365 = £109.50 | 31p × 365 = £113.15 | £113.15 | | **Gas total** | **£853.50** | **£833.15** | **£833.15** | | **Annual total** | **£2,401.75** | **£2,262.15** | **£2,035.35** | | Compared with E | +£366.40 | +£226.80 | n/a | Gas costs the same on V and E, so all of E's advantage over V comes from electricity. The car is what makes E the winner. On last year's usage alone, E would cost £109.20 *more* than V. ## How robust is the result? - **Less car charging than expected.** Every kWh charged off-peak costs 8p on E and 22p on V, so E saves 14p per kWh. E overtakes V once off-peak car charging reaches 109.20 ÷ 0.14 = **780 kWh**, which is about a third of the estimate. - **Some charging slips into peak hours.** Each kWh moved from off-peak to peak adds 22p to E's bill (30p − 8p). - E stays cheaper than V unless more than about **1,030 kWh** of car charging is at peak. Put the other way, at least about 1,370 kWh must be charged off-peak. - E stays cheaper than F unless more than about **1,665 kWh** is at peak. - **V's rates change.** V only wins if the supplier *cuts* its prices. Over the full year, the electricity unit rate would need to fall from 22p to about **17.9p**, a cut of 4.1p. With 30 days' notice, a cut would cover at most about 11 months, so it would need to be larger still. A rise would only widen E's lead. E is fixed, so it is also the more predictable option. - **The off-peak window is long enough.** 2,400 kWh a year is about 6.6 kWh a night. - A 7 kW home charger delivers that in about an hour. - A standard 3-pin plug at about 2.3 kW delivers about 11.5 kWh in the 5-hour window, which is still enough on average. - **There are no exit fees.** If the car arrives late or charging habits turn out differently, the household can switch again at no cost. ## Recommendation **Switch to the Time-of-use tariff (E). It saves about £227 over the year compared with staying on V, and it fixes prices for 12 months.** To get that saving, the household should: - **Check the meter.** Time-of-use tariffs normally need a smart meter that can record peak and off-peak use separately. - **Set the car to charge only between 00:30 and 05:30.** Keep the dishwasher and washing machine timers as they are. - **Check the first couple of bills.** If more than about a third of the car's charging is showing as peak use, review the tariff choice. Switching is free. Review it critically and produce an improved version.

# Energy Tariff Comparison for the Next 12 Months ## Answer **The Time-of-use tariff (E) is cheapest at £2,035.35 for the year.** - It is **£226.80 cheaper than staying on Variable (V)**, which costs £2,262.15. - It is **£366.40 cheaper than Fixed (F)**, which costs £2,401.75. The household should switch to E. The saving depends on charging the car off-peak, but the margin is large enough to absorb a lot of slippage. ## Usage for the next 12 months | | Peak | Off-peak | Total | |---|---|---|---| | Existing use (3,100 kWh, 15% off-peak) | 2,635 | 465 | 3,100 | | Car charging (all off-peak) | 0 | 2,400 | 2,400 | | **Total electricity** | **2,635** | **2,865** | **5,500** | | Gas (unchanged) | | | 12,000 | ## Costs (365 days) | | Fixed (F) | Variable (V) | Time-of-use (E) | |---|---|---|---| | Electricity units | 5,500 × 24.5p = £1,347.50 | 5,500 × 22.0p = £1,210.00 | 2,635 × 30p = £790.50
2,865 × 8p = £229.20 | | Electricity standing charge | 55p × 365 = £200.75 | 60p × 365 = £219.00 | 50p × 365 = £182.50 | | **Electricity total** | **£1,548.25** | **£1,429.00** | **£1,202.20** | | Gas units | 12,000 × 6.2p = £744.00 | 12,000 × 6.0p = £720.00 | 12,000 × 6.0p = £720.00 | | Gas standing charge | 30p × 365 = £109.50 | 31p × 365 = £113.15 | 31p × 365 = £113.15 | | **Gas total** | **£853.50** | **£833.15** | **£833.15** | | **Annual total** | **£2,401.75** | **£2,262.15** | **£2,035.35** | | Compared with E | +£226.80 more than V… see below | | | | | F | V | E | |---|---|---|---| | Extra cost compared with E | £366.40 | £226.80 | n/a | **Why E wins:** - Gas costs the same on V and E, so all of E's advantage comes from electricity. - The car is what makes the difference. On last year's usage alone, E would cost **£109.20 more** than V, because the household's existing peak use costs 30p on E against 22p on V. - Each kWh of off-peak car charging costs 8p on E and 22p on V, a saving of 14p. Over 2,400 kWh that saves £336, which more than covers E's £109.20 penalty. - F is never cheaper than V on these rates. It costs £139.60 more whatever the usage pattern, because both are flat-rate tariffs and F is dearer on every line except the electricity standing charge. ## How robust is the result? | Risk | E stays cheapest as long as… | How likely is it to fail? | |---|---|---| | Less car charging than expected | Off-peak car charging is at least **780 kWh** (£109.20 ÷ 14p) | Low. That is about a third of the estimate. | | Some charging happens at peak | No more than about **1,030 kWh** of car charging is at peak. Each kWh moved to peak adds 22p to E's bill. | Low, if the charging is scheduled. At least 1,370 kWh of the 2,400 must be off-peak. | | V's rates are cut | V's electricity rate stays above about **17.9p** for the whole year (a £226.80 cut spread over 5,500 kWh) | Low. No change has been announced, and with 30 days' notice a cut could cover at most about 11 months, so it would need to be deeper still. A rise in V's rates only widens E's lead. | **The car arrives next week, not today.** That means about 51 weeks of charging, or roughly 2,350 kWh rather than 2,400. This trims E's saving by about £6, to roughly **£220**. The ranking does not change. **F only becomes the best choice if two things go wrong at once:** - More than about 1,665 kWh of charging happens at peak, so that F beats E. - V's rates rise by enough to make V dearer than F. Even then, the household could switch away because there are no exit fees. **The off-peak window is long enough.** 2,400 kWh a year averages about 6.6 kWh a night. - A 7 kW charger delivers that in about an hour. - A 3-pin plug at about 2.3 kW delivers about 11.5 kWh in the 5-hour window. That covers the average, but a very depleted battery may need more than one night. ## Recommendation **Switch to Time-of-use (E).** It saves about £220–£227 over the year compared with staying on V, and it fixes prices for 12 months. To get the saving, the household should: 1. **Check the meter.** E needs a smart meter that records peak and off-peak use separately. 2. **Confirm the off-peak hours with the supplier.** Some tariffs keep 00:30–05:30 in GMT, which means 01:30–06:30 in summer. Set the car and appliance timers to match. 3. **Set the car to charge only in the off-peak window.** Keep the dishwasher and washing machine timers as they are. 4. **Check the first couple of bills.** If more than about 40% of the car's charging is showing as peak use, review the tariff. Switching is free. --- ### Review notes: what I changed and why - **All figures re-verified.** The totals, the £780 kWh threshold, the 1,030 and 1,665 kWh peak thresholds and the 17.9p threshold are all correct. - **Removed the "what changed" changelog** from the body. It was about earlier drafts, not the household's decision. - **Added that F is always dearer than V** (by £139.60). This makes the narrow conditions under which F could win much clearer. - **Folded the late-arrival adjustment into the headline** as about £220. Previously it was mentioned but not quantified. - **Corrected the bill-check trigger.** "A third" of charging at peak (about 800 kWh) was more cautious than the real break-even of about 1,030 kWh, which is about 43%. I changed it to about 40%. - **Added a check on GMT versus BST off-peak times.** This is a common practical pitfall that could quietly push charging into peak hours. - **Noted that the 3-pin plug covers the average night but not every night.**
